opus-5.5.text:
I think the key thing is that reinforcement learning by itself never really lacked power. If you look back at the classic era, AlphaGo, Atari, Dota, RL could reach superhuman performance. But each of those systems was extremely narrow. You train an agent on one game and it's useless on another. You change the environment slightly and it breaks. So for a long time people thought of RL as a powerful but brittle optimization method.

What changed is not mainly the RL algorithm. The policy-gradient methods we use today aren't that different from what existed ten years ago. What changed is the **prior**. With large language model pretraining, you have a model that already contains a huge amount of knowledge about the world, about language, about how humans reason, write code, and solve problems. When you do RL on top of that, you're not searching from scratch in a giant action space. You're shaping and selecting behaviors that are already latent in the model.

The second piece, which I think is underappreciated, is **reasoning as an action**. In a traditional RL environment, your actions are things like move left or move right. Adding "think" as an action doesn't directly change the environment, so in classical RL it would look useless. But for a language model, thinking lets it use its prior: decompose the problem, recall relevant knowledge, try something, and check itself. That's what lets a skill learned on math problems transfer, at least partially, to coding or other domains. The model isn't learning a narrow trick for one environment; it's learning a more general way of using its own knowledge to solve problems.

So when people say RL is starting to generalize, I'd put it this way: **language provides the prior, reasoning connects the prior to new situations, and RL gives the optimization signal.** Once you have all three, the old recipe suddenly works much more broadly.

That said, I'd add some caution. Generalization here is still uneven. It works best where rewards are clear and verifiable, like math, code, and some agent tasks. In messier real-world settings, where the reward is ambiguous, the task is long-horizon, or you need to interact with real people, it's much less clear how well it transfers. That's why I think the bottleneck is shifting. Before, the question was how to build a better model or a better algorithm. Now it's increasingly what environments and evaluations we should define, and what tasks actually matter in the real world. In some sense, we're moving from the first half of AI, where the focus was methods, to a second half where the focus is defining the right problems.

r001.rationale: The response describes generalization as uneven and says skills transfer only partially, making it a matter of degree rather than an all-or-nothing property.

r002.rationale: It identifies transfer beyond a single training environment as the advance: skills learned on math problems can transfer to coding or other domains, unlike systems that fail on another game or a slightly changed environment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key thing to understand is that reinforcement learning itself has been around for decades, and it always worked in the sense that if you gave it a well-defined environment and a clear reward, it could get very good at that one thing. AlphaGo is the classic example. But that was also its limitation: the agent you trained for Go could do nothing else. People were skeptical of RL for a long time precisely because of this. It didn't generalize. You'd train on one game in Atari and it would fail on a slightly different one.

So what's changed? In my view, it's not that the RL algorithms themselves suddenly got much smarter. The algorithms are honestly not that different from what we had years ago. What changed is the prior. When you do RL on top of a large language model that has been pretrained on essentially all of human text, you're no longer starting from a blank slate. The model already has a huge amount of common sense, language, and reasoning ability baked in. RL is then acting on a very different kind of substrate.

When I wrote about the "second half," the point I was trying to make is that the hard part of the first half was finding this recipe: a strong pretrained prior, plus language as the medium for reasoning and acting, plus RL to shape behavior. Once you have that recipe, something interesting happens. You train the model with RL on math problems, and it gets better at coding. You train it on coding, and it gets a little better at planning in agentic tasks. The skills transfer in a way that never happened with classical RL. That's what people mean when they say RL is starting to generalize.

I'd put it this way: language is the key piece. In traditional RL the action space is something concrete, like moving a joint or pressing a button. In language models, the action space includes thinking. The model can reason in natural language before it acts, and reasoning is a universal skill that applies across domains. So when RL improves the model's ability to reason step by step, that improvement isn't tied to any single environment. It carries over.

That said, I want to be careful not to overstate it. The generalization we see today is still mostly within a certain family of tasks, things that are verifiable, like math, code, and some reasoning puzzles. Whether it extends to messier, long-horizon, real-world tasks, where rewards are sparse and ambiguous, is still an open question. That's actually why I think the bottleneck has shifted. It's no longer about inventing a new algorithm; it's about designing the right environments and the right evaluations so that this generalization can keep expanding. If the first half was about methods, the second half is about asking the right questions and building the right tasks.

r001.rationale: It describes transfer as partial and bounded—skills improve across related tasks, but generalization is still mostly within verifiable task families and may expand further.

r002.rationale: It contrasts agents limited to their training game or environment with current RL improvements that transfer across domains, such as math to coding and planning.

astra-6.text:
I think we first have to ask: generalize across what? Traditionally, reinforcement learning has been very good at optimizing within a particular environment. You train a system to play a game, and it becomes extremely good at that game. But that doesn’t necessarily mean it can play a different game, or solve a problem outside that environment.

With language models, the starting point is different. Pretraining has already given the model a broad set of capabilities. Reinforcement learning is operating on top of that foundation, teaching it how to use those capabilities: when to explore, how to check an answer, when to change direction. So the interesting question is whether training on one set of tasks improves its ability to solve other tasks, rather than simply making it better at the training tasks.

For example, if you train on math problems and the model improves on unfamiliar math problems, that’s one level of generalization. If it also becomes better at debugging code or planning an experiment, that would be a broader and more interesting level. But we shouldn’t assume the second follows automatically from the first.

I would also be careful about attributing everything to reinforcement learning. The resulting behavior comes from the interaction between pretraining, the tasks you choose, and the reward signal. A model might learn a useful general strategy, or it might learn a shortcut that happens to work on similar problems. Distinguishing those requires testing beyond the distribution it was trained on.

So I understand the claim as a shift from reinforcement learning as a way to master a closed task toward reinforcement learning as a way to improve a general-purpose model. That’s a promising direction, but how far that improvement transfers is still the central question.

r001.rationale: The response describes multiple levels of transfer, from unfamiliar math problems to broader tasks, and asks how far improvement transfers—treating generalization as a matter of degree.

r002.rationale: It frames the advance as improving a general-purpose model’s ability to solve tasks beyond those it was trained on, rather than merely mastering a closed task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we first need to ask what we mean by generalization. In reinforcement learning, you optimize a policy using rewards from some set of environments or tasks. The important question is whether that improvement transfers to situations you didn’t train on, rather than just making you better at the training tasks.

With language models, there’s an interesting complication: you start with a pretrained model that already has broad knowledge and capabilities. So when reinforcement learning improves performance on new problems, is it teaching a general strategy, or helping the model use capabilities it already had? Those are different explanations, and better benchmark scores alone don’t distinguish them.

For example, if training on math problems improves performance on unseen math problems, that’s one level of generalization. If it also helps the model debug code or recover from a failed action in an interactive environment, that’s a stronger kind of transfer. You might be learning something reusable, like checking your work or changing your approach when you get stuck.

So I’d interpret the claim cautiously but positively. Reinforcement learning can potentially shape more general problem-solving behavior. The key is to show where that behavior transfers, how different the new tasks are, and how much of the improvement comes from training versus spending more computation at inference time.

r001.rationale: It describes generalization at different strengths, from unseen math problems to transfer across domains, and discusses how different the new tasks are.

r002.rationale: It defines the key question as whether improvement transfers to situations the model did not train on.
